findings.title: Undisclosed visible kink in the dot matrix display's wires at the start of the move
findings.evidence: shapes42.txt, this round, beat 1: all five dot matrix wires bend more than the 100-degree 'fold or tent' threshold set in round4/scripts/README.txt (CLK 129, CS 124, VCC 113, GND 110, DIN 108 degrees, at 0.055 - 0.07, near the matrix header [649-652, 920-932, 1341-1348]). In the same beat the blended wires are only 0.87 - 0.92 times the length of either shape they blend between. On screen: after_w1000x634_Step42c_0050.png shows a sharp Z-kink in the bundle just after the matrix header; at 0100 it has become an S-bend; at 0000 the bundle is smooth. Round 3 had no matrix-wire bend over 100 degrees before 0.275. The README's 'What is left' names only the cable fold at 0.30 - 0.34 and the stand-up contacts. Lee's complaint was that the move looked 'weird'.
findings.suggestion: Smooth the change of the matrix wires from their bench shape to the spun shape near the header: match the run near the matrix by distance from the matrix end, or add an intermediate shape. Re-run shapes42.py until beat 1 stays under 100 degrees. Otherwise, state the kink in the README's Step 42 account.

verdict.reason:
I checked the finding and could not refute it.

1) Pictures. I cropped and enlarged the region at 3x. In after_w1000x634_Step42c_0050.png all five dot matrix wires (brown, green, navy, maroon, teal) form a sharp zigzag shaped like a lightning bolt, about 10-15 mm past the matrix's header. It sits in open space left of the module, on screen at about x 673-687, y 590-620 of the 1500x951 picture. In _0000 the same bundle runs smoothly from the header to the module pins. In _0100 it is a rounded hump with no corners, and in _0150 it is smooth. The 1920 and 760 pictures are taken only every 0.1, so they cannot show 0.05. after_w1920x1000_Step42c_0100.png does show the same region (the matrix header at about 840,680) in clear view and well away from the caption box, so the kink would show at that size too.

2) Numbers. shapes42.txt for this round, beat 1, gives the sharpest bends as CLK 129, CS 124, VCC 113, GND 110 and DIN 108 degrees, at 0.055-0.07. The length ratios are x0.867-0.915. The scripts README treats any bend over 100 degrees in 3 mm as a fold or tent. Using steps.json, I placed the kink 12-13 mm from the a-end (NAUO138) of routes 154, 180 and 181. It falls inside route 154's b_whole=16.76 mm transition zone, which matches the picture. motion_Step42c_final.txt has the matrix CLK and CS wires going into NAUO282 (the USB plug) and NAUO78 (the module) by 1.3-2.1 mm at 0.08-0.10, close by in space ([652, 927, 1337] against the kink at [649-652, 920-932, 1341-1348]).

3) Round 3. Its matrix wires stay at or under 80 degrees until 0.275, which is what the finding says. Round 3 did reach 122-129 degrees at 0.275-0.345, though. So the fold was moved to the opening of the step, not removed.

4) Disclosure. The README's fourth-round Step 42 account says the tent was fixed ("now, while the module spins flat, they turn to come straight up out of their pins"). Its "What is left" names only the contacts, the stand-up crossings and the cable fold at 0.30-0.34 (about 0.15 s). It does not mention this kink. Grepping guide.py's diff, the README and the scripts README for kink, zigzag or fold-related wording turns up nothing about it. By the README's own standard (a 0.15 s cable fold is disclosed), this one should be too.

5) Impact. The glitch is brief, roughly 0.1-0.25 s of the 4 s step, and it does not mislead anyone about assembly. But it happens in plain view at the very start of Step 42, the step Lee called "a mess" and "weird", so it bears directly on Lee's request.

findings.title: The module does not pass cleanly through the gap, and the README understates the contacts
findings.evidence: motion_Step42c_final.txt, beat 1, while the USB end swings through the corner between the matrix wires and the blue button's wires: matrix CLK 2.10 mm and CS 1.28 mm into the USB plug (NAUO282) at 0.08; CLK 1.69, CS 1.42 and DIN 0.48 mm into the module (NAUO78) at 0.10. The USB cable also goes 1.44 mm into H10 (NAUO64) and 0.66 mm into H11 (NAUO62) at 0.09, and 0.56 mm into the Nano at 0.12. Six button wires go 0.54 - 1.38 mm into the module at 0.29. The README reports 96 contacts but itemises only the deepest (2.1 mm) and the 54 + 28 wire-against-wire ones. It does not mention the cable passing into the case parts H10 and H11, although guide.py's own comment says the cable's way was chosen to stop it going through the case's back corner.
findings.suggestion: List the 14 into-part contacts in the README, especially the cable into H10 and H11. Or widen the swing or the A end's lift in beat 1 so that the USB end clears the matrix wires and the cable clears H10 and H11, which is what Lee meant by 'through the gap'.

verdict.reason:
The finding's numbers are right, but neither part of it holds up as a real problem.

What checks out: docs/research/pmg/round4/verify/motion_Step42c_final.txt has exactly the contacts it cites. There are 14 contacts into parts and 82 between wires, 96 in all. The 82 split into 54 between bundles (all button against button) and 28 within a bundle (10 of the matrix's, 6 of the 4-digit display's, 3 each for the black, blue, white and yellow buttons). Among the 14 are the USB cable 1.44 mm into H10 (NAUO64) and 0.66 mm into H11 (NAUO62), both at 0.09, and six button wires into the module (NAUO78) at 0.29. The README's Step 42 account names only the total, the deepest contact (matrix CLK 2.1 mm into the USB plug, first beat), the 54 and the 28. It does not name the other 13 contacts into parts.

Why it is not a real defect:

(1) The README is not wrong. Its total (96), its timing ("all in the first two beats"; every contact falls between 0.08 and 0.34) and its deepest value (2.10 mm) are all accurate. That 2.1 mm limit covers every contact it leaves unnamed: the deepest of those is 1.69 mm, and the cable is 1.44 mm into H10. It also already says, as left over, that the matrix's wire passes into the USB plug in the first beat. That is the substance of "does not pass cleanly through the gap".

(2) The H10 contact is not new, and guide.py does not claim it is gone. Round 3's final check (docs/research/pmg/round3/verify3/motion_check_201.txt) already had "usb cable into NAUO64 1.31 mm". The guide.py comment says only that an alternative route, round the case's side, went through the case's back corner. It does not say the chosen route never touches the case.

(3) None of these contacts can be seen in the pictures. I looked at after_w1000x634_Step42c_0050/0100/0150/0200/0300 and after_w1920x1000_Step42c_0000/0100/0200, zoomed in. At 0.10 the matrix wires arch over the module's top-left beside the plug and run behind the board's edge, which looks physically plausible. Where the cable crosses H4's back face beside the plug, it is drawn in front of the protruding tab, with no visible clipping. At 0.30 the button wires pass behind the board, which faces the camera, so the 0.29 contacts are hidden. These contacts are 0.5 - 2.1 mm deep and last about 0.1 - 0.15 s at a scale of roughly 3 - 4 px per mm.

(4) Lee's request is met in broad strokes. The module swings up between the matrix's bundle and the buttons' bundles. The cable rises with it and ends between the black button's wires and the display's (after_w1000x634_Step42c_1000.png).

What remains is a matter of how complete the README is, not something a student would see, nor a failure of Lee's request.

verdict.reason:
The finding describes the picture correctly. It is not a defect against Lee's request.

What I checked:

  - The display wires are 10-19 mm to the cable's left on screen and 16-32 mm nearer the camera.
  - The black button's wires are 17-34 mm to its left and 5-20 mm further away.
  - The finding leaves out that, lower down, the black button's three wires pass behind the cable on screen (cable points 89-113, 23-91 mm behind). The display's four wires cross in front just below that (points 114-119, about 31-34 mm in front). So the cable is sandwiched between the two along the line of sight. It does not show because the black button's wires are hidden behind the cable and the case.

Why this is not a problem:
- The cable's final shape is byte-identical to round 3's. Route 186 matches HEAD's steps.json exactly (max difference 0.0), and so do the wires. That end is also where Step 43 starts.

So "letting it settle between the Black Push button's wires and the 4-digit display's wires" most likely names where it should end up, not a new end. In 3D it does lie between them: the black button's wires behind it, the display's in front.
- Lee asked for Step 42 to be seen from straight behind. From there, "between" is along the line of sight, so it cannot show as side by side. That comes from the camera Lee chose, not from a wrong placement.
- The README says the cable ends "between the black button's wires and the display's". That is accurate in 3D, and the README does not claim it reads that way from behind.
- A student is not affected: the caption only asks them to lay the A end on the table behind the case, and the picture shows that.

At most this is worth a sentence to Lee. It is not a defect in the work.

findings.title: At the LMS's size, the close-ups cover part of the module or have long leaders across it
findings.evidence: after_w1000x634_Step17c.png and Step18c.png: the close-up's right edge is at x about 468 and hides the module's left end (the DC jack and the board corner), which before_w1000x634_Step17c.png shows. In after_w1000x634_Step19c.png and Step20c.png the leader runs about 420 px (about 28% of the width) straight across the module and its headers to the pin. At 1440 and 1920 wide the 17c close-up clears the module.
findings.suggestion: Optional: at 1000 wide, a smaller close-up or another side for 17c and 18c would keep the module whole. The rulebook only forbids covering labels and eyes, so this is a judgement call.

verdict.reason:
I checked both halves of the finding. One half doesn't hold up. The other is real, and on a stronger footing than the finding gives it.

1) Steps 17c and 18c at the LMS's size (1000 x 634): the observation is right, but it isn't a defect. In after_w1000x634_Step17c.png and after_w1000x634_Step18c.png the close-up's right edge is at about x 468 (of 1500). It covers the module's DC jack and its left board corner, which before_w1000x634_Step17c.png shows. The step is about the S8 and S9 pins, though. Those, the cap boxed in red and the pin's ring are all in clear view, and the jack plays no part in the step. At 1440 the close-up clears the module (after_w1440x714_Step17c.png). At 760 it sits below the module (after_w760x720_Step17c.png). This part is a matter of taste.

2) Steps 19c and 20c: real, and at every window size, not only at 1000. The close-up is placed on the right. Its leader runs straight across the I/O module, its Nano Board's headers and its yellow pin headers to V9 or G9, which are at the module's left edge in this view:
- 1000 wide: from x about 978 to about 558 of 1500 (about 28%), in after_w1000x634_Step19c.png and Step20c.png.
- 1440 wide: from about 1290 to about 800 of 2000, in after_w1440x714_Step19c.png.
- 1920 wide: from about 1318 to about 740, in after_w1920x1000_Step20c.png.
- 760 wide: from about 770 to about 350 of 1140, in after_w760x720_Step19c.png.

This breaks a rule Lee set the day before. docs/cadasio-patterns.md, lines 131-132 (In-house, Lee, 2026-10-20): "a close-up sits on the side of the part its leader goes to, so that the leader does not cross the part". The finding's claim that the rulebook only forbids covering labels and eyes is therefore wrong.

Why it happens: the player puts a close-up on the side with the most room (player/js/player.js, buildInset) unless the step asks for a side. The inset in guide.py (line 528) gives no side, and steps.json's insets for 19c and 20c have no "side" key.

There was room on the left. At 1000 the space left of the module, below the caption box, is empty (x 0-450, y 410-800), and at 1440 and 1920 there is far more. A close-up placed left would have a short leader that does not cross the module. At 760 there is no room on the left.

The fourth-round section of the README (PMG Build Instructions/README.txt) doesn't mention this, or that the rule was broken, as CLAUDE.md asks ("If a kit needs to break a rule, say which one and why").

It is low severity: the dashed ring still marks the right pin, and a student can follow the line. It matters mostly as a conflict with a convention Lee has stated.
